*Title*: Big Data Analytics Services for Enhancing Business Intelligence

*Abstract*: This article examines how to use big data analytics services to enhance business intelligence (BI). More specifically, this article proposes an ontology of big data analytics and presents a big data analytics service-oriented architecture (BASOA), and then applies BASOA to BI, where our surveyed data analysis shows that the proposed BASOA is viable for enhancing BI and enterprise information systems. This article also explores temporality, expectability, and relativity as the characteristics of intelligence in BI. These characteristics are what customers and decision makers expect from BI in terms of systems, products, and services of organizations. The proposed approach in this article might facilitate the research and development of business analytics, big data analytics, and BI as well as big data science and big data computing.

# Dataset:

    -	Gender of the participant surveyed on these topics
    -	Temporality: an average score of the rated ability to adapt to change over time 1 (not changing) to 7 (changing a lot)
    -	Expectability: a rated degree of satisfaction with the BI
    -	Relativity: average score rating of how much better one system is than another in BI 1 (not very good) to 7 (very good)
    -	Positive emotion: how positive participants felt about BI (higher scores are more positive, ranges from 1 to 7).

# Data Screening:

## Accuracy: 

    a.	Include output that indicates if the data are or are not accurate.
    b.	If the data are not accurate, delete the inaccurate scores.
    c.	Include a summary that shows that you fixed the inaccurate scores.
    
```
I loaded the data and identified out-of-range values in relativity (< -2 or > 10) and positive emotion (< -1 or > 8). I created a copy called notypos and documented the initial missing data counts. I then replaced all inaccurate values with NA to remove them from analysis. Finally, I verified the cleaning by reporting how many values were corrected and confirming the new missing data counts.
```
    
```{r accuracy}
# Load the data
master <- read.csv("07_data.csv")

# Find out-of-range values for relativity
relativity_outliers <- which(master$relativity < -2 | master$relativity > 10)
if(length(relativity_outliers) > 0) {
  cat("Relativity out of range (< -2 or > 10):\n")
  print(master[relativity_outliers, c("gender", "relativity")])
  cat("\n")
}

# Find out-of-range values for positive emotion
positive_outliers <- which(master$positive < -1 | master$positive > 8)
if(length(positive_outliers) > 0) {
  cat("Positive emotion out of range (< -1 or > 8):\n")
  print(master[positive_outliers, c("gender", "positive")])
  cat("\n")
}

# Create a cleaned dataset
notypos <- master

cat("Before cleaning:\n")
cat("  Total observations:", nrow(notypos), "\n")
cat("  Missing in relativity:", sum(is.na(notypos$relativity)), "\n")
cat("  Missing in positive:", sum(is.na(notypos$positive)), "\n\n")

# Set out-of-range values to NA
notypos$relativity[notypos$relativity < -2 | notypos$relativity > 10] <- NA
notypos$positive[notypos$positive < -1 | notypos$positive > 8] <- NA

cat("Inaccurate values set to NA (missing)\n")
cat("  Relativity: Set", length(relativity_outliers), "out-of-range values to NA\n")
cat("  Positive: Set", length(positive_outliers), "out-of-range values to NA\n\n")

cat("After cleaning:\n")
cat("  Total observations:", nrow(notypos), "\n")
cat("  Missing in relativity:", sum(is.na(notypos$relativity)), "\n")
cat("  Missing in positive:", sum(is.na(notypos$positive)), "\n\n")
```
    
## Missing:

    a.  Since any accuracy errors will create more than 5% missing data, exclude all data pairwise for the rest of the analyses. 
    
```
I calculated the total number of data points in the dataset by multiplying the number of rows by the number of columns. I then counted how many cells contain missing values (NA) across the entire dataset and calculated what percentage of all data points are missing.
```
    
```{r missing}
# Determine if we have more than 5% missing overall
total_cells <- nrow(notypos) * ncol(notypos)
total_missing <- sum(is.na(notypos))
overall_missing_percent <- (total_missing / total_cells) * 100

cat("OVERALL MISSING DATA:\n")
cat("Total data points:", total_cells, "\n")
cat("Missing data points:", total_missing, "\n")
cat("Percentage missing:", sprintf("%.2f%%", overall_missing_percent), "\n\n")
```
    
## Outliers:

    a.	Include a summary of your mahal scores.
    b.	What are the df for your Mahalanobis cutoff?
    c.	What is the cut off score for your Mahalanobis measure?
    d.	How many outliers did you have? 
    
```
I calculated Mahalanobis distances for all four continuous variables (temporality, expectability, relativity, positive). df for Mahalanobis cutoff is 4. I used a conservative cutoff of p < .001 from the chi-square distribution, which gave me a cutoff score of 18.4668. I identified and removed the outliers, creating a cleaned dataset called noout.
```
    
```{r outliers}
continuous_vars <- c("temporality", "expectability", "relativity", "positive")
mahal_data <- notypos[, continuous_vars]
mahal_complete <- na.omit(mahal_data)

mahal <- mahalanobis(mahal_complete, 
                     colMeans(mahal_complete), 
                     cov(mahal_complete))

# a. Include a summary of your Mahalanobis scores
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

print(summary(mahal))

cat("Distribution of Mahalanobis distances:\n")
hist(mahal, 
     breaks = 30, 
     main = "Distribution of Mahalanobis Distances",
     xlab = "Mahalanobis Distance",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "white")

# b. What are the df for your Mahalanobis cutoff?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

df_mahal <- ncol(mahal_complete)

cat("Degrees of freedom (df) = number of variables in the analysis\n")
cat("  Variables:", paste(continuous_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("  df =", df_mahal, "\n\n")

# c. What is the cut off score for your Mahalanobis measure?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

cutoff <- qchisq(1 - 0.001, df_mahal)

cat("Using the chi-square distribution with df =", df_mahal, "\n")
cat("Significance level: p < .001 (conservative threshold)\n\n")
cat("Cutoff score:", sprintf("%.4f", cutoff), "\n\n")

# d. How many outliers did you have?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

outliers <- mahal > cutoff
num_outliers <- sum(outliers)

cat("Outlier identification:\n")
cat("  Cases with Mahalanobis distance >", sprintf("%.4f", cutoff), ":", num_outliers, "\n")
cat("  Percentage of sample:", sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * num_outliers / length(mahal)), "\n\n")

if(num_outliers > 0) {
  cat("Outlier case details:\n")
  outlier_indices <- which(outliers)
  outlier_mahal <- mahal[outliers]
  
  outlier_summary <- data.frame(
    Case = outlier_indices,
    Mahalanobis_Distance = outlier_mahal,
    Exceeds_Cutoff_By = outlier_mahal - cutoff
  )
  
  print(outlier_summary)
  
  cat("\n\nOutlier data values:\n")
  print(mahal_complete[outliers, ])
  
} else {
  cat("✓ No multivariate outliers detected at p < .001 threshold.\n")
}

# Create dataset without outliers
noout <- mahal_complete[!outliers, ]

cat("Dataset after removing outliers:\n")
cat("  Original complete cases:", nrow(mahal_complete), "\n")
cat("  Cases removed:", num_outliers, "\n")
cat("  Final sample size:", nrow(noout), "\n")
cat("  Percentage retained:", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nrow(noout) / nrow(mahal_complete)), "\n\n")

if(num_outliers > 0) {
  cat("Multivariate outliers have been identified and removed.\n")
  cat("The dataset 'noout' contains", nrow(noout), "cases without outliers.\n")
} else {
  cat("No multivariate outliers detected. All cases retained.\n")
  cat("The dataset 'noout' is identical to the complete cases.\n")
}

# Q-Q plot of Mahalanobis distances against chi-square distribution
qqplot(qchisq(ppoints(length(mahal)), df = df_mahal), mahal,
       main = "Q-Q Plot: Mahalanobis Distance vs Chi-Square Distribution",
       xlab = "Theoretical Chi-Square Quantiles",
       ylab = "Observed Mahalanobis Distance",
       pch = 19,
       col = ifelse(outliers, "red", "blue"))
abline(0, 1, col = "gray", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(h = cutoff, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", 
       legend = c("Normal cases", "Outliers", "Expected (y=x)", "Cutoff"),
       col = c("blue", "red", "gray", "red"),
       pch = c(19, 19, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, 2, 2),
       lwd = c(NA, NA, 2, 2))

```
    
# Assumptions:

## Linearity: 

    a.	Include a picture that shows how you might assess multivariate linearity.
    b.	Do you think you've met the assumption for linearity? 

```
I assessed the linearity assumption by creating scatterplot matrices and comparing linear regression lines (red) to LOESS smooth curves (blue) for all variable pairs. For each variable pair, I calculated the correlation between linear and LOESS predictions and compared their RMSE values—high correlation (>0.95) and minimal RMSE improvement (<10%).

Expectability vs Temporality:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.9050
  RMSE improvement with loess: 1.27%
  Assessment: ~ MOSTLY LINEAR - minor deviations acceptable

Relativity vs Temporality:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.6945
  RMSE improvement with loess: 3.19%
  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected

Positive vs Temporality:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.5528
  RMSE improvement with loess: 4.64%
  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected

Relativity vs Expectability:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.8470
  RMSE improvement with loess: 1.37%
  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected

Positive vs Expectability:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.0895
  RMSE improvement with loess: 1.51%
  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected

Positive vs Relativity:
  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): 0.3952
  RMSE improvement with loess: 1.48%
  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected

Variable pairs meeting linearity: 1 out of 6 (16.7%)

✗ LINEARITY ASSUMPTION VIOLATED

Conclusion:
  Substantial non-linear relationships detected.
```

```{r linearity}
# a. Include a picture that shows how you might assess multivariate linearity
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Load required package
if(!require(psych)) {
  install.packages("psych")
  library(psych)
}

# METHOD 1: Scatterplot Matrix with Correlation Coefficients

pairs.panels(noout[, c("temporality", "expectability", "relativity", "positive")],
             method = "pearson",
             hist.col = "lightblue",
             density = TRUE,
             ellipses = FALSE,
             lm = TRUE,
             main = "Scatterplot Matrix: Assessing Linearity")

# METHOD 2: Individual Scatterplots with Regression and Loess Lines

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

plot_linearity <- function(x, y, xname, yname) {
  plot(x, y,
       pch = 19,
       col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
       main = paste(yname, "vs", xname),
       xlab = xname,
       ylab = yname,
       cex = 0.8)
  
  abline(lm(y ~ x), col = "red", lwd = 2)
  lines(lowess(x, y), col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
  legend("topleft", 
         legend = c("Linear", "Loess smooth"),
         col = c("red", "blue"),
         lty = c(1, 2),
         lwd = 2,
         cex = 0.7,
         bg = "white")
}

plot_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$expectability, "Temporality", "Expectability")
plot_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$relativity, "Temporality", "Relativity")
plot_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$positive, "Temporality", "Positive")
plot_linearity(noout$expectability, noout$relativity, "Expectability", "Relativity")
plot_linearity(noout$expectability, noout$positive, "Expectability", "Positive")
plot_linearity(noout$relativity, noout$positive, "Relativity", "Positive")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 3: Residual Plots from Fake Regression

set.seed(123)
noout$random_y <- rnorm(nrow(noout))

fake_model <- lm(random_y ~ temporality + expectability + relativity + positive, 
                 data = noout)

standardized_residuals <- rstandard(fake_model)
fitted_values <- fitted(fake_model)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Plot 1: Residuals vs Fitted
plot(fitted_values, standardized_residuals,
     pch = 19,
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values",

     ylab = "Standardized Residuals",
     ylim = c(-3, 3))
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(-2, 2), col = "orange", lty = 2)
lines(lowess(fitted_values, standardized_residuals), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
text(min(fitted_values), 2.5, "Look for: Random scatter around zero", 
     adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = "darkgreen")

# Plot 2: Residuals vs Temporality
plot(noout$temporality, standardized_residuals,
     pch = 19,
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
     main = "Residuals vs Temporality",
     xlab = "Temporality",
     ylab = "Standardized Residuals",
     ylim = c(-3, 3))
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(-2, 2), col = "orange", lty = 2)
lines(lowess(noout$temporality, standardized_residuals), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

# Plot 3: Residuals vs Expectability
plot(noout$expectability, standardized_residuals,

     main = "Residuals vs Expectability",

abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(-2, 2), col = "orange", lty = 2)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

# Plot 4: Residuals vs Relativity
plot(noout$relativity, standardized_residuals,
     pch = 19,
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
     main = "Residuals vs Relativity",
     xlab = "Relativity",
     ylab = "Standardized Residuals",
     ylim = c(-3, 3))
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(h = c(-2, 2), col = "orange", lty = 2)
lines(lowess(noout$relativity, standardized_residuals), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# b. Do you think you've met the assumption for linearity?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

check_linearity <- function(x, y, xname, yname) {
  linear_fit <- lm(y ~ x)
  loess_fit <- loess(y ~ x)
  
  linear_pred <- predict(linear_fit)
  loess_pred <- predict(loess_fit)
  
  pred_cor <- cor(linear_pred, loess_pred)
  
  linear_rmse <- sqrt(mean((y - linear_pred)^2))
  loess_rmse <- sqrt(mean((y - loess_pred)^2))
  rmse_improvement <- ((linear_rmse - loess_rmse) / linear_rmse) * 100
  
  cat(sprintf("%s vs %s:\n", yname, xname))
  cat(sprintf("  Correlation (linear vs loess predictions): %.4f\n", pred_cor))
  cat(sprintf("  RMSE improvement with loess: %.2f%%\n", rmse_improvement))
  
  if(pred_cor > 0.95 & rmse_improvement < 10) {
    cat("  Assessment: ✓ LINEAR - loess and linear very similar\n\n")
    return(TRUE)
  } else if(pred_cor > 0.85 & rmse_improvement < 20) {
    cat("  Assessment: ~ MOSTLY LINEAR - minor deviations acceptable\n\n")
    return(TRUE)
  } else {
    cat("  Assessment: ✗ NON-LINEAR - substantial curvature detected\n\n")
    return(FALSE)
  }
}

# Check all pairs
linearity_results <- c()
linearity_results[1] <- check_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$expectability, 
                                        "Temporality", "Expectability")
linearity_results[2] <- check_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$relativity, 
                                        "Temporality", "Relativity")
linearity_results[3] <- check_linearity(noout$temporality, noout$positive, 
                                        "Temporality", "Positive")
linearity_results[4] <- check_linearity(noout$expectability, noout$relativity, 
                                        "Expectability", "Relativity")
linearity_results[5] <- check_linearity(noout$expectability, noout$positive, 
                                        "Expectability", "Positive")
linearity_results[6] <- check_linearity(noout$relativity, noout$positive, 
                                        "Relativity", "Positive")

percent_linear <- mean(linearity_results) * 100

cat(sprintf("Variable pairs meeting linearity: %d out of 6 (%.1f%%)\n\n", 
            sum(linearity_results), percent_linear))

if(percent_linear >= 80) {
  cat("✓ LINEARITY ASSUMPTION MET\n\n")
} else if(percent_linear >= 50) {
  cat("~ LINEARITY PARTIALLY MET\n\n")
} else {
  cat("✗ LINEARITY ASSUMPTION VIOLATED\n\n")
  cat("Conclusion:\n")
  cat("  Substantial non-linear relationships detected.\n")
}

```

```{r normality}
# a. Include a picture that shows how you might assess multivariate normality
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Load required packages
if(!require(moments)) {
  install.packages("moments")
  library(moments)
}

# METHOD 1: Histograms with Normal Curve Overlay

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))
plot_histogram <- function(data, varname) {
  h <- hist(data, 
            breaks = 20,
            main = paste("Histogram:", varname),
            xlab = varname,
            ylab = "Frequency",
            col = "lightblue",
            border = "white",
            xlim = c(min(data) - 0.5*sd(data), max(data) + 0.5*sd(data)))
  
  xfit <- seq(min(data), max(data), length = 100)
  yfit <- dnorm(xfit, mean = mean(data), sd = sd(data))
  yfit <- yfit * diff(h$mids[1:2]) * length(data)
  lines(xfit, yfit, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  
  abline(v = mean(data), col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  
  legend("topright", 
         legend = c("Normal curve", "Mean"),
         col = c("red", "blue"),
         lty = c(1, 2),
         lwd = 2,
         cex = 0.8,
         bg = "white")
}

plot_histogram(noout$temporality, "Temporality")
plot_histogram(noout$expectability, "Expectability")
plot_histogram(noout$relativity, "Relativity")
plot_histogram(noout$positive, "Positive Emotion")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 2: Q-Q Plots (Quantile-Quantile Plots)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))

plot_qq <- function(data, varname) {
  qqnorm(data, 
         main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", varname),
         xlab = "Theoretical Quantiles",
         ylab = "Sample Quantiles",
         pch = 19,
         col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
         cex = 0.8)
  qqline(data, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  
  n <- length(data)
  sorted_data <- sort(data)
  theoretical <- qnorm(ppoints(n))
  
  se <- (sd(data) / sqrt(n)) * sqrt(ppoints(n) * (1 - ppoints(n)))
  
  grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
  
  text(min(theoretical), max(sorted_data),
       "Points should fall\non red line",
       adj = c(0, 1),
       cex = 0.8,
       col = "darkgreen")
}

plot_qq(noout$temporality, "Temporality")
plot_qq(noout$expectability, "Expectability")
plot_qq(noout$relativity, "Relativity")
plot_qq(noout$positive, "Positive Emotion")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 3: Density Plots with Normal Comparison

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))

plot_density <- function(data, varname) {
  d <- density(data)
  plot(d, 
       main = paste("Density Plot:", varname),
       xlab = varname,
       ylab = "Density",
       lwd = 2,
       col = "blue")
  
  xfit <- seq(min(data), max(data), length = 100)
  yfit <- dnorm(xfit, mean = mean(data), sd = sd(data))
  lines(xfit, yfit, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  
  polygon(d, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2), border = NA)
  
  legend("topright",
         legend = c("Actual", "Normal"),
         col = c("blue", "red"),
         lty = c(1, 2),
         lwd = 2,
         cex = 0.8,
         bg = "white")
  
  grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
}

plot_density(noout$temporality, "Temporality")
plot_density(noout$expectability, "Expectability")
plot_density(noout$relativity, "Relativity")
plot_density(noout$positive, "Positive Emotion")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 4: Combined Diagnostic Plot

create_diagnostic <- function(data, varname) {
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))
  
  # 1. Histogram
  h <- hist(data, breaks = 20, main = paste(varname, "- Histogram"),
            xlab = varname, col = "lightblue", border = "white")
  xfit <- seq(min(data), max(data), length = 100)
  yfit <- dnorm(xfit, mean = mean(data), sd = sd(data))
  yfit <- yfit * diff(h$mids[1:2]) * length(data)
  lines(xfit, yfit, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  
  # 2. Q-Q Plot
  qqnorm(data, main = paste(varname, "- Q-Q Plot"),
         pch = 19, col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5))
  qqline(data, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  
  # 3. Boxplot
  boxplot(data, main = paste(varname, "- Boxplot"),
          ylab = varname, col = "lightgreen", horizontal = FALSE)
  
  # 4. Density plot
  d <- density(data)
  plot(d, main = paste(varname, "- Density"),
       xlab = varname, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
  xfit <- seq(min(data), max(data), length = 100)
  yfit <- dnorm(xfit, mean = mean(data), sd = sd(data))
  lines(xfit, yfit, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  polygon(d, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.2), border = NA)
  
  par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
}

cat("Detailed diagnostic plots for each variable:\n\n")
create_diagnostic(noout$temporality, "Temporality")
create_diagnostic(noout$expectability, "Expectability")
create_diagnostic(noout$relativity, "Relativity")
create_diagnostic(noout$positive, "Positive Emotion")

# b. Do you think you've met the assumption for normality?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
normality_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(),
  N = numeric(),
  Mean = numeric(),
  SD = numeric(),
  Skewness = numeric(),
  Kurtosis = numeric(),
  Shapiro_W = numeric(),
  Shapiro_p = numeric(),
  Assessment = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Function to assess normality
assess_normality <- function(data, varname) {
  n <- length(data)
  m <- mean(data)
  s <- sd(data)
  skew <- skewness(data)
  kurt <- kurtosis(data) - 3  # Excess kurtosis
  
  # Shapiro-Wilk test (for n <= 5000)
  if(n <= 5000) {
    shapiro_test <- shapiro.test(data)
    w_stat <- shapiro_test$statistic
    p_val <- shapiro_test$p.value
  } else {
    w_stat <- NA
    p_val <- NA
  }
  
  # Assessment criteria
  # Skewness: |skew| < 2 is acceptable, < 1 is good
  # Kurtosis: |kurt| < 7 is acceptable, < 3 is good
  # Shapiro: p > 0.05 suggests normality
  
  skew_ok <- abs(skew) < 2
  kurt_ok <- abs(kurt) < 7
  shapiro_ok <- is.na(p_val) || p_val > 0.05
  
  if(skew_ok && kurt_ok && shapiro_ok) {
    assessment <- "✓ NORMAL"
  } else if((abs(skew) < 3 && abs(kurt) < 10 && (is.na(p_val) || p_val > 0.01)) || n > 50) {
    assessment <- "~ ACCEPTABLE"
  } else {
    assessment <- "✗ NON-NORMAL"
  }
  
  cat(sprintf("%s:\n", varname))
  cat(sprintf("  N: %d\n", n))
  cat(sprintf("  Mean: %.3f, SD: %.3f\n", m, s))
  cat(sprintf("  Skewness: %.3f %s\n", skew, 
              ifelse(abs(skew) < 1, "(✓ good)", 
                     ifelse(abs(skew) < 2, "(~ acceptable)", "(✗ problematic)"))))
  cat(sprintf("  Kurtosis: %.3f %s\n", kurt,
              ifelse(abs(kurt) < 3, "(✓ good)",
                     ifelse(abs(kurt) < 7, "(~ acceptable)", "(✗ problematic)"))))
  if(!is.na(w_stat)) {
    cat(sprintf("  Shapiro-Wilk: W = %.4f, p = %.4f %s\n", w_stat, p_val,
                ifelse(p_val > 0.05, "(✓ normal)", "(✗ reject normality)")))
  }
  cat(sprintf("  Overall: %s\n\n", assessment))
  
  return(data.frame(
    Variable = varname,
    N = n,
    Mean = m,
    SD = s,
    Skewness = skew,
    Kurtosis = kurt,
    Shapiro_W = w_stat,
    Shapiro_p = p_val,
    Assessment = assessment,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

# Assess each variable
normality_results <- rbind(normality_results,
                           assess_normality(noout$temporality, "Temporality"))
normality_results <- rbind(normality_results,
                           assess_normality(noout$expectability, "Expectability"))
normality_results <- rbind(normality_results,
                           assess_normality(noout$relativity, "Relativity"))
normality_results <- rbind(normality_results,
                           assess_normality(noout$positive, "Positive Emotion"))

cat("SUMMARY TABLE:\n")
cat("--------------\n")
print(normality_results, row.names = FALSE)

normal_count <- sum(grepl("NORMAL|ACCEPTABLE", normality_results$Assessment))
total_vars <- nrow(normality_results)

cat(sprintf("Variables meeting normality: %d out of %d (%.1f%%)\n\n",
            normal_count, total_vars, 100 * normal_count / total_vars))

if(normal_count == total_vars) {
  cat("✓ NORMALITY ASSUMPTION FULLY MET\n\n")
} else if(normal_count >= total_vars * 0.75) {
  cat("✓ NORMALITY ASSUMPTION REASONABLY MET\n\n")
} else if(nrow(noout) >= 30) {
  cat("~ NORMALITY ASSUMPTION PARTIALLY MET\n\n")
} else {
  cat("✗ NORMALITY ASSUMPTION VIOLATED\n\n")
}
```

## Homogeneity and Homoscedasticity: 

    a.	Include a picture that shows how you might assess multivariate homogeneity.
    b.	Do you think you've met the assumption for homogeneity?
    c.	Do you think you've met the assumption for homoscedasticity?
    
```
I created boxplots by gender to compare variance, calculated variance ratios, and generated spread-location plots. For statistical testing, I performed Levene's test on each variable to assess whether variances differ significantly between women and men. To assess homoscedasticity, I examined residual plots and scale-location plots from a regression model. I also conducted the Breusch-Pagan test. 

Variables meeting homogeneity: 4 out of 4

✓ HOMOGENEITY ASSUMPTION MET
Breusch-Pagan Test:
  BP = 1.3013, p = 0.8612
  Result: ✓ Homoscedastic

✓ HOMOSCEDASTICITY ASSUMPTION MET
```
    
```{r homogs}

# METHOD 1: Boxplots by Gender for Each Variable
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))

plot_boxplot <- function(data, var_col, varname) {
  women_data <- data[data$gender == "women", var_col]
  men_data <- data[data$gender == "men", var_col]
  
  women_data <- women_data[!is.na(women_data)]
  men_data <- men_data[!is.na(men_data)]
  
  if(length(women_data) == 0 | length(men_data) == 0) {
    cat("ERROR: No data for", varname, "\n")
    return()
  }
  
  bp <- boxplot(women_data, men_data,
                main = paste(varname, "by Gender"),
                xlab = "Gender",
                ylab = varname,
                col = c("pink", "lightblue"),
                names = c("Women", "Men"),
                outline = TRUE)
  
  points(jitter(rep(1, length(women_data)), amount = 0.1),
         women_data,
         pch = 19,
         col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.3),
         cex = 0.5)
  
  points(jitter(rep(2, length(men_data)), amount = 0.1),
         men_data,
         pch = 19,
         col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3),
         cex = 0.5)
  
  grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
  
  var_women <- var(women_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  var_men <- var(men_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  ratio <- max(var_women, var_men) / min(var_women, var_men)
  
  text(1.5, min(bp$stats) + 0.1 * diff(range(bp$stats)),
       sprintf("Var ratio: %.2f", ratio),
       cex = 0.8,
       col = ifelse(ratio < 2, "darkgreen", "darkred"))
}

plot_boxplot(noout, "temporality", "Temporality")
plot_boxplot(noout, "expectability", "Expectability")
plot_boxplot(noout, "relativity", "Relativity")
plot_boxplot(noout, "positive", "Positive Emotion")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 2: Variance Comparison Plots

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# METHOD 3: Spread-Location Plots by Gender
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))

create_spread_plot <- function(data, varname) {
  women_data <- data[data$gender == "women", varname]
  men_data <- data[data$gender == "men", varname]
  
  women_data <- women_data[!is.na(women_data)]
  men_data <- men_data[!is.na(men_data)]
  
  women_mean <- mean(women_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  men_mean <- mean(men_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  women_abs_dev <- abs(women_data - women_mean)
  men_abs_dev <- abs(men_data - men_mean)
  
  plot(c(rep(1, length(women_abs_dev)), rep(2, length(men_abs_dev))),
       c(women_abs_dev, men_abs_dev),
       pch = 19,
       col = c(rep(rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.3), length(women_abs_dev)),
               rep(rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.3), length(men_abs_dev))),
       xlim = c(0.5, 2.5),
       xaxt = "n",
       main = paste(varname, "- Spread Plot"),
       xlab = "Gender",
       ylab = "Absolute Deviation from Group Mean")
  
  axis(1, at = c(1, 2), labels = c("Women", "Men"))
  
  segments(0.7, median(women_abs_dev, na.rm = TRUE),
           1.3, median(women_abs_dev, na.rm = TRUE),
           col = "red", lwd = 3)
  segments(1.7, median(men_abs_dev, na.rm = TRUE),
           2.3, median(men_abs_dev, na.rm = TRUE),
           col = "blue", lwd = 3)
  
  grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
}

lines(lowess(fitted_vals, standardized_resid), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
text(min(fitted_vals), 2.5,
     "Look for: Even spread\nacross fitted values",
     adj = 0, cex = 0.7, col = "darkgreen")

# Plot 2: Scale-Location plot
sqrt_abs_resid <- sqrt(abs(standardized_resid))
plot(fitted_vals, sqrt_abs_resid,
     pch = 19,
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.5),
     main = "Scale-Location Plot",

lines(lowess(fitted_vals, sqrt_abs_resid), col = "red", lwd = 2)
grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)
text(min(fitted_vals), max(sqrt_abs_resid) * 0.9,
     "Flat red line = \nhomoscedastic",

# b. Do you think you've met the assumption for homogeneity?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
homogeneity_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(),
  F_statistic = numeric(),
  p_value = numeric(),
  Var_Women = numeric(),
  Var_Men = numeric(),
  Var_Ratio = numeric(),
  Assessment = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

perform_levene <- function(data, varname) {
  formula_str <- paste(varname, "~ gender")
  levene_result <- leveneTest(as.formula(formula_str), data = data)
  
  f_stat <- levene_result$`F value`[1]
  p_val <- levene_result$`Pr(>F)`[1]
  
  var_w <- var(data[data$gender == "women", varname], na.rm = TRUE)
  var_m <- var(data[data$gender == "men", varname], na.rm = TRUE)
  var_ratio <- max(var_w, var_m) / min(var_w, var_m)
  
  if(p_val > 0.05 && var_ratio < 2) {
    assessment <- "✓ HOMOGENEOUS"
  } else if(p_val > 0.01 || var_ratio < 3) {
    assessment <- "~ ACCEPTABLE"
  } else {
    assessment <- "✗ HETEROGENEOUS"
  }
  
  cat(sprintf("%s:\n", varname))
  cat(sprintf("  Levene's F = %.4f, p = %.4f %s\n",
              f_stat, p_val,
              ifelse(p_val > 0.05, "(✓)", "(✗)")))
  cat(sprintf("  Variance - Women: %.4f, Men: %.4f\n", var_w, var_m))
  cat(sprintf("  Variance Ratio: %.4f %s\n", var_ratio,
              ifelse(var_ratio < 2, "(✓)", "(high)")))
  cat(sprintf("  Assessment: %s\n\n", assessment))
  
  return(data.frame(
    Variable = varname,
    F_statistic = f_stat,
    p_value = p_val,
    Var_Women = var_w,
    Var_Men = var_m,
    Var_Ratio = var_ratio,
    Assessment = assessment,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

homogeneity_results <- rbind(homogeneity_results,
                             perform_levene(noout, "temporality"))
homogeneity_results <- rbind(homogeneity_results,
                             perform_levene(noout, "expectability"))
homogeneity_results <- rbind(homogeneity_results,
                             perform_levene(noout, "relativity"))
homogeneity_results <- rbind(homogeneity_results,
                             perform_levene(noout, "positive"))

cat("SUMMARY TABLE:\n")
print(homogeneity_results, row.names = FALSE)

homog_count <- sum(grepl("HOMOGENEOUS|ACCEPTABLE", homogeneity_results$Assessment))
total_tests <- nrow(homogeneity_results)

cat(sprintf("Variables meeting homogeneity: %d out of %d\n\n", homog_count, total_tests))

if(homog_count == total_tests) {
  cat("✓ HOMOGENEITY ASSUMPTION MET\n")
} else if(homog_count >= 3) {
  cat("✓ HOMOGENEITY ASSUMPTION REASONABLY MET\n")
} else {
  cat("⚠ HOMOGENEITY ASSUMPTION PARTIALLY MET\n")
}

# c. Do you think you've met the assumption for homoscedasticity?

  cat("  Result: ✓ Homoscedastic\n\n")
  cat("✓ HOMOSCEDASTICITY ASSUMPTION MET\n")
} else {
  cat("  Result: ✗ Heteroscedastic\n\n")
  cat("⚠ HOMOSCEDASTICITY ASSUMPTION VIOLATED\n")
}
```

# Hypothesis Testing / Graphs:

Create a scatter plot of temporality and relativity.

    a.	Be sure to check x/y axis labels and length.
    b.	What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have?

```
I created a scatterplot examining the relationship between temporality and relativity. I added reference lines at the means, displayed the correlation coefficient and sample size, and included a grid for readability. To assess the relationship type, I calculated Pearson's correlation, performed significance testing, and determined effect size using Cohen's guidelines. I compared linear regression predictions to LOESS predictions to assess linearity. 

The scatter plot reveals a weak POSITIVE relationship between temporality (ability to adapt to change over time) and relativity (system comparison rating) in the Business Intelligence context. However, the relationship is too weak to draw strong conclusions about the association between these two characteristics of business intelligence systems.
```

```{r plot1}

y_range <- range(noout$relativity, na.rm = TRUE)

y_limits <- c(y_range[1] - y_padding, y_range[2] + y_padding)

abline(h = mean(noout$relativity, na.rm = TRUE),

cor_value <- cor(noout$temporality, noout$relativity,

legend("topleft",

legend("bottomright",

       bty = "n",

       text.col = "darkgray")

# b. What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
cor_test <- cor.test(noout$temporality, noout$relativity, 
                     method = "pearson",
                     use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cat("Pearson's correlation:\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$estimate), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_test$parameter, ") =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$p.value))

if(cor_test$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_test$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_test$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat(" (not significant)\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$conf.int[1]), ",",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

# Effect size interpretation
cat("Effect size interpretation (Cohen, 1988):\n")
abs_r <- abs(cor_test$estimate)
if(abs_r < 0.1) {
  effect_size <- "Negligible (|r| < 0.1)"
} else if(abs_r < 0.3) {
  effect_size <- "Small (0.1 ≤ |r| < 0.3)"
} else if(abs_r < 0.5) {
  effect_size <- "Medium (0.3 ≤ |r| < 0.5)"
} else {
  effect_size <- "Large (|r| ≥ 0.5)"
}
cat("  ", effect_size, "\n\n")

# Coefficient of determination

cat("Coefficient of determination:\n")

cat("  Interpretation:", sprintf("%.2f%%", r_squared * 100),

}

loess_fit <- loess(relativity ~ temporality, data = noout)

loess_pred <- predict(loess_fit)

  cat("  considerable error.\n\n")

  cat("  Temporality appears to be a meaningful predictor of relativity.\n\n")
}

cat("Linearity: ", linearity, "\n", sep = "")
if(pred_cor > 0.95) {

  cat("  A linear model is appropriate for these data.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("  There may be some curvature in the relationship.\n")
  cat("  Consider examining residual plots or non-linear models.\n\n")
}

cat("Statistical significance:\n")
if(cor_test$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  The relationship is statistically significant (p < .05).\n")
  cat("  We can reject the null hypothesis that r = 0.\n")
  cat("  The observed correlation is unlikely to be due to chance alone.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("  The relationship is NOT statistically significant (p ≥ .05).\n")
  cat("  We cannot reject the null hypothesis that r = 0.\n")
  cat("  The observed correlation could plausibly be due to chance.\n\n")
}

cat("The scatter plot reveals a", strength, direction, "relationship between\n")
cat("temporality (ability to adapt to change over time) and relativity (system\n")
cat("comparison rating) in the Business Intelligence context.\n\n")

if(abs(cor_test$estimate) >= 0.3 && cor_test$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("This suggests that participants who rate BI systems as better at adapting\n")
  cat("to change over time also tend to rate", 
      ifelse(cor_test$estimate > 0, "those systems as", "different systems as"), "\n")
  cat(ifelse(cor_test$estimate > 0, "better in comparison", "having mixed comparisons"), 
      "to other systems.\n")
} else {
  cat("However, the relationship is", ifelse(cor_test$p.value >= 0.05, "not significant or", ""), 
      "too weak to draw\n")
  cat("strong conclusions about the association between these two characteristics\n")
  cat("of business intelligence systems.\n")
}
```

Create a scatter plot of expectability and positive emotion.

    a.	Include a linear line on the graph. 
    b.	Be sure to check x/y axis labels and length.
    c.	What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have?

```
I created a scatterplot of expectability and positive emotion. I fitted a linear regression model and added a red regression line to the plot along with the equation, correlation coefficient, and R². To assess the relationship, I calculated Pearson's correlation. I compared linear predictions to LOESS predictions to confirm linearity. 

The scatter plot with linear regression line reveals a negligible or no NEGATIVE relationship between expectability (satisfaction with BI) and positive emotion (positivity about BI). However, the relationship is not statistically significant or weak, suggesting that satisfaction with BI and positive emotions about BI, while potentially related, may also be influenced by other independent factors not captured in this simple bivariate analysis.
```

```{r plot2}
# a. Include a linear line on the graph
# b. Be sure to check x/y axis labels and length
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

x_range <- range(noout$expectability, na.rm = TRUE)
y_range <- range(noout$positive, na.rm = TRUE)

x_padding <- diff(x_range) * 0.1
y_padding <- diff(y_range) * 0.1

x_limits <- c(x_range[1] - x_padding, x_range[2] + x_padding)
y_limits <- c(y_range[1] - y_padding, y_range[2] + y_padding)

plot(noout$expectability, 
     noout$positive,
     main = "Relationship between Expectability and Positive Emotion",
     xlab = "Expectability\n(Satisfaction with Business Intelligence)",
     ylab = "Positive Emotion\n(Positivity about BI: 1-7 scale)",
     xlim = x_limits,
     ylim = y_limits,

     cex = 1.2,
     cex.lab = 1.1,
     cex.axis = 1.0,
     cex.main = 1.3)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

linear_model <- lm(positive ~ expectability, data = noout)

abline(linear_model, col = "red", lwd = 3)

intercept <- coef(linear_model)[1]
slope <- coef(linear_model)[2]

equation_text <- sprintf("y = %.3fx + %.3f", slope, intercept)
legend("topleft", 
       legend = equation_text,
       bty = "n",
       cex = 1.1,
       text.col = "red",
       text.font = 2)

cor_value <- cor(noout$expectability, noout$positive, 
                 use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson")

r_squared <- summary(linear_model)$r.squared
legend("bottomright",
       legend = c(sprintf("r = %.3f", cor_value),
                  sprintf("R² = %.3f", r_squared)),
       bty = "n",
       cex = 1.1,
       text.col = "darkblue",
       text.font = 2)

n_complete <- sum(complete.cases(noout[, c("expectability", "positive")]))
text(x_limits[1] + 0.05 * diff(x_limits), 
     y_limits[2] - 0.05 * diff(y_limits),
     sprintf("n = %d", n_complete),
     cex = 1.0,
     col = "darkgray",
     adj = 0)

# c. What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
cor_test <- cor.test(noout$expectability, noout$positive, 
                     method = "pearson",
                     use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cat("Pearson's correlation:\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$estimate), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_test$parameter, ") =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$p.value))

if(cor_test$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_test$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_test$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat(" (not significant)\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$conf.int[1]), ",",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

reg_summary <- summary(linear_model)
cat("Coefficients:\n")
cat("  Slope:", sprintf("%.4f", slope), 
    "(SE =", sprintf("%.4f", reg_summary$coefficients[2, 2]), ")\n\n")

cat("Model fit:\n")
cat("  R² =", sprintf("%.4f", r_squared), "\n")
cat("  Adjusted R² =", sprintf("%.4f", reg_summary$adj.r.squared), "\n")
cat("  F(", reg_summary$fstatistic[2], ",", reg_summary$fstatistic[3], ") =",
    sprintf("%.4f", reg_summary$fstatistic[1]), 
    ", p =", sprintf("%.4f", pf(reg_summary$fstatistic[1], 
                               reg_summary$fstatistic[2], 
                               reg_summary$fstatistic[3], 
                               lower.tail = FALSE)), "\n\n", sep = "")

# Effect size interpretation
cat("Effect size interpretation (Cohen, 1988):\n")
abs_r <- abs(cor_test$estimate)
if(abs_r < 0.1) {
  effect_size <- "Negligible (|r| < 0.1)"
} else if(abs_r < 0.3) {
  effect_size <- "Small (0.1 ≤ |r| < 0.3)"
} else if(abs_r < 0.5) {
  effect_size <- "Medium (0.3 ≤ |r| < 0.5)"
} else {
  effect_size <- "Large (|r| ≥ 0.5)"
}
cat("  ", effect_size, "\n\n")

# c. Relationship type description
if(abs(cor_test$estimate) < 0.1) {
  strength <- "negligible or no"
} else if(abs(cor_test$estimate) < 0.3) {
  strength <- "weak"
} else if(abs(cor_test$estimate) < 0.5) {
  strength <- "moderate"
} else {
  strength <- "strong"
}

if(cor_test$estimate > 0) {
  direction <- "POSITIVE"
  direction_desc <- "As expectability (satisfaction) increases, positive emotion tends to increase"
} else {
  direction <- "NEGATIVE"
  direction_desc <- "As expectability (satisfaction) increases, positive emotion tends to decrease"
}

# Check linearity by examining residuals
residuals <- resid(linear_model)
fitted_vals <- fitted(linear_model)

# Test for non-linearity using runs test or visual inspection
loess_fit <- loess(positive ~ expectability, data = noout)
loess_pred <- predict(loess_fit)
linear_pred <- fitted(linear_model)

pred_cor <- cor(linear_pred, loess_pred, use = "complete.obs")

if(pred_cor > 0.98) {
  linearity <- "STRONGLY LINEAR"
  linearity_desc <- "The red line fits the data very well with minimal curvature"
} else if(pred_cor > 0.95) {
  linearity <- "LINEAR"
  linearity_desc <- "The red line fits the data well"
} else if(pred_cor > 0.90) {
  linearity <- "MOSTLY LINEAR"
  linearity_desc <- "The red line fits reasonably well with some scatter"
} else {
  linearity <- "POTENTIALLY NON-LINEAR"
  linearity_desc <- "The data may show some curvature"
}

cat("Relationship type:", direction, "-", strength, "-", linearity, "\n\n")

cat("Direction: ", direction, "\n", sep = "")
cat("  ", direction_desc, ".\n", sep = "")
cat("  The regression line has a", ifelse(slope > 0, "positive", "negative"), 
    "slope of", sprintf("%.4f", slope), ".\n\n")

cat("Strength: ", toupper(strength), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  The correlation coefficient r = ", sprintf("%.3f", cor_test$estimate),

if(abs(cor_test$estimate) < 0.3) {

  cat("  Points are widely scattered, indicating that expectability alone is not\n")

} else if(abs(cor_test$estimate) < 0.5) {
  cat("  The scatter plot shows a noticeable trend with moderate scatter.\n")
  cat("  While there is a clear tendency, individual predictions based on\n")
  cat("  expectability alone would have considerable error.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("  The scatter plot shows points clustering closely around the regression line.\n")
  cat("  Expectability appears to be a meaningful predictor of positive emotion.\n")
  cat("  Individual predictions would be reasonably accurate.\n\n")
}

cat("Linearity: ", linearity, "\n", sep = "")
cat("  ", linearity_desc, ".\n", sep = "")
if(pred_cor > 0.95) {
  cat("  A straight line is an appropriate model for this relationship.\n")
  cat("  No evidence of curvature or non-linear patterns.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("  Some deviation from perfect linearity may be present.\n")
  cat("  The linear model is still reasonable but may not capture all patterns.\n\n")
}

cat("Fit quality:\n")
cat("  The linear regression line explains", sprintf("%.2f%%", r_squared * 100),

if(r_squared > 0.25) {
  cat("  This is a substantial amount of explained variance.\n\n")
} else if(r_squared > 0.09) {

cat("Statistical significance:\n")

}

cat("The scatter plot with linear regression line reveals a", strength, direction, "\n")

cat("(positivity about BI).\n\n")

if(abs(cor_test$estimate) >= 0.3 && cor_test$p.value < 0.05) {
```

Create a scatter plot of expectability and relativity, grouping by gender.

    a.	Include a linear line on the graph. 
    b.	Be sure to check x/y axis labels and length.
    c.	What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have for each group?
    
```
I created a scatterplot comparing the expectability-relativity relationship for women (red circles with red regression line) and men (blue triangles with blue regression line) on the same axes for direct comparison. For each gender group separately, I calculated Pearson correlations, regression slopes and R² values, and classified the relationship strength (weak/moderate/strong) and direction (positive/negative). To compare groups, I performed Fisher's Z-test to determine if the correlations differ significantly between women and men. 

The correlations differ significantly between gender groups (p < .05).
Among women, the relationship between expectability and relativity isnegligible and not statistically significant.
Among men, there is a moderate positive relationship between satisfaction with BI (expectability) and system comparison ratings (relativity).
The relationship between expectability and relativity differs significantly between gender groups. Women show a negligible positive relationship (r = 0.053), while men show a moderate positive relationship(r = 0.423).
```
    
```{r plot3}
# a. Include a linear line on the graph
# b. Be sure to check x/y axis labels and length
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
x_range <- range(noout$expectability, na.rm = TRUE)
y_range <- range(noout$relativity, na.rm = TRUE)

y_limits <- c(y_range[1] - y_padding, y_range[2] + y_padding)

women_data <- noout[noout$gender == "women", ]
men_data <- noout[noout$gender == "men", ]

plot(noout$expectability, 
     noout$relativity,
     type = "n",  # Don't plot points yet
     main = "Relationship between Expectability and Relativity by Gender",

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

points(women_data$expectability,
       women_data$relativity,
       pch = 19,
       col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),  # Semi-transparent red
       cex = 1.2)

women_model <- lm(relativity ~ expectability, data = women_data)
abline(women_model, col = "red", lwd = 3)

points(men_data$expectability,
       men_data$relativity,
       pch = 17,  # Triangle
       col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.5),  # Semi-transparent blue
       cex = 1.2)

men_model <- lm(relativity ~ expectability, data = men_data)
abline(men_model, col = "blue", lwd = 3)

women_slope <- coef(women_model)[2]
women_intercept <- coef(women_model)[1]
men_slope <- coef(men_model)[2]
men_intercept <- coef(men_model)[1]

legend("topleft",
       legend = c(
         "Women",

       lty = c(NA, 1, NA, 1),
       lwd = c(NA, 3, NA, 3),
       cex = 0.9,
       bty = "n")

cor_women <- cor(women_data$expectability, women_data$relativity, 
                 use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_men <- cor(men_data$expectability, men_data$relativity, 
               use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

legend("bottomright",
       legend = c(
         sprintf("Women: r = %.3f", cor_women),
         sprintf("Men: r = %.3f", cor_men)
       ),
       text.col = c("red", "blue"),
       bty = "n",
       cex = 1.0,

# c. What type of relationship do these two variables appear to have for each group?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
cor_test_women <- cor.test(women_data$expectability, women_data$relativity,
                           method = "pearson")

cat("Correlation analysis:\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$estimate), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_test_women$parameter, ") =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$p.value))
if(cor_test_women$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_test_women$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_test_women$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat(" (not significant)\n")
}
cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$conf.int[1]), ",",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

women_summary <- summary(women_model)
cat("Linear regression:\n")
cat("  Slope:", sprintf("%.4f", women_slope), "(SE =", 
    sprintf("%.4f", women_summary$coefficients[2, 2]), ")\n")
cat("  Interpretation: For every 1-unit increase in expectability,\n")
cat("                  relativity", ifelse(women_slope > 0, "increases", "decreases"),
    "by", sprintf("%.4f", abs(women_slope)), "units.\n")
cat("  R² =", sprintf("%.4f", women_summary$r.squared), 
    sprintf("(%.2f%% variance explained)\n\n", women_summary$r.squared * 100))

if(abs(cor_test_women$estimate) < 0.1) {
  women_strength <- "negligible"
} else if(abs(cor_test_women$estimate) < 0.3) {
  women_strength <- "weak"
} else if(abs(cor_test_women$estimate) < 0.5) {
  women_strength <- "moderate"
} else {
  women_strength <- "strong"
}

women_direction <- ifelse(cor_test_women$estimate > 0, "positive", "negative")

cat("Relationship type: ", toupper(women_direction), " - ", 
    toupper(women_strength), "\n\n", sep = "")

cor_test_men <- cor.test(men_data$expectability, men_data$relativity,
                         method = "pearson")

cat("Correlation analysis:\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$estimate), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_test_men$parameter, ") =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$p.value))
if(cor_test_men$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_test_men$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_test_men$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat(" (not significant)\n")
}
cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$conf.int[1]), ",",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

men_summary <- summary(men_model)
cat("Linear regression:\n")
cat("  Slope:", sprintf("%.4f", men_slope), "(SE =", 
    sprintf("%.4f", men_summary$coefficients[2, 2]), ")\n")
cat("  Interpretation: For every 1-unit increase in expectability,\n")
cat("                  relativity", ifelse(men_slope > 0, "increases", "decreases"),
    "by", sprintf("%.4f", abs(men_slope)), "units.\n")
cat("  R² =", sprintf("%.4f", men_summary$r.squared), 
    sprintf("(%.2f%% variance explained)\n\n", men_summary$r.squared * 100))

if(abs(cor_test_men$estimate) < 0.1) {
  men_strength <- "negligible"
} else if(abs(cor_test_men$estimate) < 0.3) {
  men_strength <- "weak"
} else if(abs(cor_test_men$estimate) < 0.5) {
  men_strength <- "moderate"
} else {
  men_strength <- "strong"
}

men_direction <- ifelse(cor_test_men$estimate > 0, "positive", "negative")

cat("Relationship type: ", toupper(men_direction), " - ", 
    toupper(men_strength), "\n\n", sep = "")

# c. Comparison between groups
comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Characteristic = c("Direction", "Strength", "Correlation (r)", 
                     "Slope", "R²", "Significance"),
  Women = c(
    toupper(women_direction),
    toupper(women_strength),
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_women$estimate),
    sprintf("%.4f", women_slope),
    sprintf("%.4f", women_summary$r.squared),
    ifelse(cor_test_women$p.value < 0.05, "Yes (p < .05)", "No (p ≥ .05)")
  ),
  Men = c(
    toupper(men_direction),
    toupper(men_strength),
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_men$estimate),
    sprintf("%.4f", men_slope),
    sprintf("%.4f", men_summary$r.squared),
    ifelse(cor_test_men$p.value < 0.05, "Yes (p < .05)", "No (p ≥ .05)")
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(comparison_table, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\n")

# Fisher's Z transformation to compare independent correlations
z_women <- 0.5 * log((1 + cor_test_women$estimate) / (1 - cor_test_women$estimate))
z_men <- 0.5 * log((1 + cor_test_men$estimate) / (1 - cor_test_men$estimate))

n_women <- sum(complete.cases(women_data[, c("expectability", "relativity")]))
n_men <- sum(complete.cases(men_data[, c("expectability", "relativity")]))

se_diff <- sqrt(1/(n_women - 3) + 1/(n_men - 3))
z_obs <- (z_women - z_men) / se_diff
p_value_diff <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_obs)))

cat("Fisher's Z-test comparing correlations:\n")
cat("  Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_obs), "\n")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.4f", p_value_diff), "\n\n")

if(p_value_diff < 0.05) {
  cat("  Result: The correlations differ significantly between gender groups (p < .05).\n")
} else {
  cat("  Result: The correlations do NOT differ significantly (p ≥ .05).\n")
}

if(women_strength %in% c("moderate", "strong") && cor_test_women$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  Among women, there is a", women_strength, women_direction, 
      "relationship between\n")
  cat("  satisfaction with BI (expectability) and system comparison ratings (relativity).\n")
} else {
  cat("  Among women, the relationship between expectability and relativity is\n")
  cat("  ", women_strength, " and ", 
      ifelse(cor_test_women$p.value >= 0.05, "not statistically significant", 
             "statistically significant but weak"), ".\n", sep = "")
}

cat("MEN:\n")
if(men_strength %in% c("moderate", "strong") && cor_test_men$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  Among men, there is a", men_strength, men_direction, 
      "relationship between\n")
  cat("  satisfaction with BI (expectability) and system comparison ratings (relativity).\n")
} else {
  cat("  Among men, the relationship between expectability and relativity is\n")
  cat("  ", men_strength, " and ", 
      ifelse(cor_test_men$p.value >= 0.05, "not statistically significant", 
             "statistically significant but weak"), ".\n", sep = "")
}

similar_direction <- women_direction == men_direction
similar_strength <- abs(cor_test_women$estimate - cor_test_men$estimate) < 0.2
significantly_different <- p_value_diff < 0.05

if(similar_direction && similar_strength && !significantly_different) {
  cat("Both women and men show similar", women_direction, women_strength, 
      "relationships\n")
  cat("between expectability and relativity.\n")
} else if(significantly_different) {
  cat("The relationship between expectability and relativity differs significantly\n")
  cat("between gender groups. Women show a", women_strength, women_direction, 
      "relationship\n")
  cat("(r =", sprintf("%.3f", cor_test_women$estimate), 
      "), while men show a", men_strength, men_direction, "relationship\n")
  cat("(r =", sprintf("%.3f", cor_test_men$estimate), 
      ").\n")
} else {
  cat("While both groups show", women_direction, "relationships, the strength differs\n")
  cat("somewhat between women (", women_strength, ", r = ", 
      sprintf("%.3f", cor_test_women$estimate), ") and\n", sep = "")
  cat("men (", men_strength, ", r = ", sprintf("%.3f", cor_test_men$estimate), 
      "), though not significantly.\n", sep = "")
}
```

Include a correlation table of all of the variables (cor).

    a.	Include the output for Pearson.
    b.	Include the output for Spearman.
    c.	Include the output for Kendall.
    d.	Which correlation was the strongest?
    e.  For the correlations with gender, would point biserial or biserial be more appropriate?  Why?
    
```
I calculated correlation matrices using three methods for all variables. I computed Pearson correlations measuring linear relationships, Spearman correlations based on ranks for monotonic relationships, and Kendall's tau for ordinal associations. For each method, I displayed the correlation coefficients, p-values for significance testing, and formatted tables with significance stars (*** p<.001, ** p<.01, * p<.05). 

Stringest correlations were: 

Pearson's r:
  Variables: Gender × Temporality 
  Correlation: r = -0.8343 
  Absolute value: |r| = 0.8343 

Spearman's ρ:
  Variables: Gender × Temporality 
  Correlation: ρ = -0.8346 
  Absolute value: |ρ| = 0.8346 

Kendall's τ:
  Variables: Gender × Temporality 
  Correlation: τ = -0.6827 
  Absolute value: |τ| = 0.6827 

For the point-biserial versus biserial question, I explained that point-biserial is appropriate because gender is a truly dichotomous variable (naturally binary), not an artificially created split of a continuous variable. The Pearson correlations with gender (coded 0/1) are mathematically equivalent to point-biserial correlations, measuring whether women and men differ on the continuous BI variables and indicating which gender scores higher.
```
    
```{r correl1}
# Create numeric version of gender
noout$gender_numeric <- ifelse(noout$gender == "women", 0, 1)

# Select variables for correlation

get_cor_pvalues <- function(data, method = "pearson") {
  n_vars <- ncol(data)
  p_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_vars, ncol = n_vars)
  
  for(i in 1:n_vars) {
    for(j in 1:n_vars) {
      if(i == j) {
        p_matrix[i, j] <- NA
      } else {
        test_result <- cor.test(data[, i], data[, j], 
                                method = method,
                                use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
        p_matrix[i, j] <- test_result$p.value
      }
    }
  }
  
  return(p_matrix)
}

    if(i != j && !is.na(pearson_p[i, j])) {
      if(pearson_p[i, j] < 0.001) {
        pearson_formatted[i, j] <- paste0(sprintf("%.4f", pearson_cor[i, j]), "***")
      } else if(pearson_p[i, j] < 0.01) {
        pearson_formatted[i, j] <- paste0(sprintf("%.4f", pearson_cor[i, j]), "** ")
      } else if(pearson_p[i, j] < 0.05) {
        pearson_formatted[i, j] <- paste0(sprintf("%.4f", pearson_cor[i, j]), "*  ")
      } else {
        pearson_formatted[i, j] <- sprintf("%.4f", pearson_cor[i, j])
      }
    } else if(i == j) {
      pearson_formatted[i, j] <- "1.0000"
    }
  }
}

# d. Which correlation was the strongest?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
find_strongest <- function(cor_matrix, matrix_name) {
  # Set diagonal to NA
  diag(cor_matrix) <- NA
  
  # Get upper triangle only (to avoid duplicates)
  cor_matrix[lower.tri(cor_matrix)] <- NA
  
  # Find maximum absolute value
  max_abs <- max(abs(cor_matrix), na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Find position of maximum
  max_pos <- which(abs(cor_matrix) == max_abs, arr.ind = TRUE)
  
  # Get the actual correlation value
  max_cor <- cor_matrix[max_pos[1], max_pos[2]]
  
  # Get variable names
  var_names <- c("Gender", "Temporality", "Expectability", "Relativity", "Positive")
  var1 <- var_names[max_pos[1]]
  var2 <- var_names[max_pos[2]]
  
  return(list(
    var1 = var1,
    var2 = var2,
    correlation = max_cor,
    abs_correlation = max_abs
  ))
}

# Find strongest for each method
pearson_strongest <- find_strongest(pearson_cor, "Pearson")
spearman_strongest <- find_strongest(spearman_cor, "Spearman")
kendall_strongest <- find_strongest(kendall_cor, "Kendall")

cat("Pearson's r:\n")
cat("  Variables:", pearson_strongest$var1, "×", pearson_strongest$var2, "\n")
cat("  Correlation: r =", sprintf("%.4f", pearson_strongest$correlation), "\n")
cat("  Absolute value: |r| =", sprintf("%.4f", pearson_strongest$abs_correlation), "\n\n")

cat("Spearman's ρ:\n")
cat("  Variables:", spearman_strongest$var1, "×", spearman_strongest$var2, "\n")
cat("  Correlation: ρ =", sprintf("%.4f", spearman_strongest$correlation), "\n")
cat("  Absolute value: |ρ| =", sprintf("%.4f", spearman_strongest$abs_correlation), "\n\n")

cat("Kendall's τ:\n")
cat("  Variables:", kendall_strongest$var1, "×", kendall_strongest$var2, "\n")
cat("  Correlation: τ =", sprintf("%.4f", kendall_strongest$correlation), "\n")
cat("  Absolute value: |τ| =", sprintf("%.4f", kendall_strongest$abs_correlation), "\n\n")

# Determine overall strongest
all_strongest <- c(pearson_strongest$abs_correlation,
                   spearman_strongest$abs_correlation,
                   kendall_strongest$abs_correlation)

overall_max <- max(all_strongest)

if(pearson_strongest$abs_correlation == overall_max) {
  cat("Method: PEARSON\n")
  cat("Variables:", pearson_strongest$var1, "and", pearson_strongest$var2, "\n")
  cat("Correlation:", sprintf("%.4f", pearson_strongest$correlation), "\n")
  cat("Absolute value:", sprintf("%.4f", pearson_strongest$abs_correlation), "\n\n")
  
  # Get p-value
  var_indices <- which(c("Gender", "Temporality", "Expectability", "Relativity", "Positive") %in% 
                       c(pearson_strongest$var1, pearson_strongest$var2))
  p_val <- pearson_p[var_indices[1], var_indices[2]]
  
  cat("Significance: p =", sprintf("%.4f", p_val))
  if(p_val < 0.001) cat(" ***\n\n")
  else if(p_val < 0.01) cat(" **\n\n")
  else if(p_val < 0.05) cat(" *\n\n")
  else cat("\n\n")
  
  r_sq <- pearson_strongest$correlation^2
  cat("  R² =", sprintf("%.4f", r_sq), 
      sprintf("(%.2f%% shared variance)\n", r_sq * 100))
}

cat("\n")

# e. For the correlations with gender, would point biserial or biserial be more appropriate? Why?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
gender_vars <- c("Temporality", "Expectability", "Relativity", "Positive")

cat("Point-Biserial Correlations (r_pb):\n\n")

for(i in 2:5) {
  var_name <- c("Temporality", "Expectability", "Relativity", "Positive")[i-1]
  
  r_pb <- pearson_cor[1, i]
  p_val <- pearson_p[1, i]
  
  cat(sprintf("  Gender × %s:\n", var_name))
  cat(sprintf("    r_pb = %.4f, p = %.4f", r_pb, p_val))
  
  if(p_val < 0.001) cat(" ***\n")
  else if(p_val < 0.01) cat(" **\n")
  else if(p_val < 0.05) cat(" *\n")
  else cat("\n")
  
  # Interpretation
  if(abs(r_pb) < 0.1) {
    strength <- "negligible"
  } else if(abs(r_pb) < 0.3) {
    strength <- "small"
  } else if(abs(r_pb) < 0.5) {
    strength <- "moderate"
  } else {
    strength <- "large"
  }
  
  direction <- ifelse(r_pb > 0, "Men score higher", "Women score higher")
  
  cat(sprintf("    Effect size: %s (%s)\n", strength, direction))
  cat("\n")
}
```

Calculate confidence interval for temporality and relativity.

```
I calculated the 95% confidence interval for the Pearson correlation between temporality and relativity by performing a correlation test. I reported the sample correlation coefficient (r), test statistic (t), p-value, and the lower and upper bounds of the confidence interval. I also calculated CIs at different confidence levels (90%, 95%, 99%) to show how higher confidence produces wider intervals. The CI provides both the precision of our estimate and statistical significance.
```

```{r cicorrel1}
temp_data <- noout$temporality
rel_data <- noout$relativity

complete_cases <- complete.cases(temp_data, rel_data)
temp_complete <- temp_data[complete_cases]
rel_complete <- rel_data[complete_cases]

n <- length(temp_complete)

cor_test_result <- cor.test(temp_complete, rel_complete, 
                            method = "pearson",
                            conf.level = 0.95)

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")

cat("Sample correlation coefficient:\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$estimate), "\n\n")

cat("Test statistic:\n")
cat("  t(", cor_test_result$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_test_result$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_test_result$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n\n")
} else if(cor_test_result$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n\n")
} else if(cor_test_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n\n")
} else {
  cat("\n\n")
}

cat("95% Confidence Interval:\n")
cat("  Lower bound:", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), "\n")
cat("  Upper bound:", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), "\n")
cat("  CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

# Check if CI includes zero
if(cor_test_result$conf.int[1] < 0 && cor_test_result$conf.int[2] > 0) {
  cat("Note: The confidence interval INCLUDES ZERO.\n")
  cat("      This suggests the correlation may not be significantly different from zero.\n")
  cat("      We cannot rule out the possibility of no relationship in the population.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("Note: The confidence interval DOES NOT INCLUDE ZERO.\n")
  cat("      This confirms a significant relationship exists in the population.\n")
  if(cor_test_result$conf.int[1] > 0) {
    cat("      The relationship is reliably POSITIVE.\n\n")
  } else {
    cat("      The relationship is reliably NEGATIVE.\n\n")
  }
}

# Effect size interpretation
r_value <- cor_test_result$estimate
r_squared <- r_value^2

cat("Effect size:\n")
if(abs(r_value) < 0.1) {
  effect <- "negligible"
} else if(abs(r_value) < 0.3) {
  effect <- "small"
} else if(abs(r_value) < 0.5) {
  effect <- "medium"
} else {
  effect <- "large"
}

cat("  Magnitude:", effect, "(Cohen, 1988)\n")
cat("  Coefficient of determination: R² =", sprintf("%.4f", r_squared), "\n")
cat("  Shared variance:", sprintf("%.2f%%", r_squared * 100), "\n\n")

# 90% CI
cor_90 <- cor.test(temp_complete, rel_complete, method = "pearson", conf.level = 0.90)
cat("90% Confidence Interval:\n")
cat("  [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_90$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_90$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  Width:", sprintf("%.4f", cor_90$conf.int[2] - cor_90$conf.int[1]), "\n\n")

# 95% CI (already calculated)
cat("95% Confidence Interval:\n")
cat("  [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  Width:", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2] - cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), "\n\n")

# 99% CI
cor_99 <- cor.test(temp_complete, rel_complete, method = "pearson", conf.level = 0.99)
cat("99% Confidence Interval:\n")
cat("  [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_99$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_99$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  Width:", sprintf("%.4f", cor_99$conf.int[2] - cor_99$conf.int[1]), "\n\n")

cat("Note: Higher confidence levels produce wider intervals.\n")
cat("      The 95% CI is the standard in most research contexts.\n\n")

par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

plot(1, cor_test_result$estimate,
     xlim = c(0.5, 1.5),
     ylim = c(min(cor_99$conf.int[1], -0.2), max(cor_99$conf.int[2], 1)),
     pch = 19,
     cex = 2,
     col = "darkblue",
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "Correlation Coefficient (r)",
     main = "95% Confidence Interval for Correlation\nTemporality × Relativity",
     xaxt = "n",
     cex.main = 1.3,
     cex.lab = 1.1)

arrows(1, cor_test_result$conf.int[1],
       1, cor_test_result$conf.int[2],
       angle = 90,
       code = 3,
       length = 0.1,
       lwd = 3,
       col = "darkblue")

abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

text(1, cor_test_result$estimate + 0.05,
     sprintf("r = %.4f", cor_test_result$estimate),
     pos = 3,
     cex = 1.1,
     font = 2)

text(1, cor_test_result$conf.int[1] - 0.02,
     sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]),
     pos = 1,
     cex = 0.9)

text(1, cor_test_result$conf.int[2] + 0.02,
     sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]),
     pos = 3,
     cex = 0.9)

text(1.3, 0,
     "H₀: ρ = 0",
     cex = 0.9,
     col = "red")

if(cor_test_result$conf.int[1] < 0 && cor_test_result$conf.int[2] > 0) {
  cat("  → The CI crosses zero (red line), indicating the correlation\n")
  cat("    is not significantly different from zero at α = .05.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("  → The CI does not cross zero (red line), confirming a\n")
  cat("    statistically significant correlation at α = .05.\n\n")
}

# Fisher's Z transformation
r <- cor_test_result$estimate
z <- 0.5 * log((1 + r) / (1 - r))
se_z <- 1 / sqrt(n - 3)

# 95% CI for Z
z_lower <- z - 1.96 * se_z
z_upper <- z + 1.96 * se_z

# Transform back to r
r_lower_fisher <- (exp(2 * z_lower) - 1) / (exp(2 * z_lower) + 1)
r_upper_fisher <- (exp(2 * z_upper) - 1) / (exp(2 * z_upper) + 1)

cat("Fisher's Z transformation:\n")
cat("  Sample r:", sprintf("%.4f", r), "\n")
cat("  Fisher's Z:", sprintf("%.4f", z), "\n")
cat("  SE(Z):", sprintf("%.4f", se_z), "\n\n")

cat("95% CI using Fisher's Z:\n")
cat("  Z interval: [", sprintf("%.4f", z_lower), ", ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", z_upper), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  r interval: [", sprintf("%.4f", r_lower_fisher), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", r_upper_fisher), "]\n\n", sep = "")

cat("Comparison with direct method:\n")
cat("  Direct method:  [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  Fisher's Z:     [", sprintf("%.4f", r_lower_fisher), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", r_upper_fisher), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  Difference:     [", 
    sprintf("%.4f", abs(cor_test_result$conf.int[1] - r_lower_fisher)), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", abs(cor_test_result$conf.int[2] - r_upper_fisher)), "]\n\n", sep = "")

cat("Correlation between Temporality and Relativity:\n\n")
cat("  Sample size: n =", n, "\n")
cat("  Pearson's r =", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$estimate), "\n")
cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.6f", cor_test_result$p.value), "\n")
cat("  R² =", sprintf("%.4f", r_squared), 
    sprintf("(%.2f%% shared variance)\n\n", r_squared * 100))

cat("Conclusion:\n")
if(cor_test_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat("  There is a statistically significant", 
      ifelse(r > 0, "positive", "negative"), "correlation between\n")
  cat("  temporality (ability to adapt to change) and relativity (system comparison).\n")
  cat("  We can be 95% confident the population correlation is between\n")
  cat("  ", sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[1]), " and ",
      sprintf("%.4f", cor_test_result$conf.int[2]), ".\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("  The correlation is not statistically significant at α = .05.\n")
  cat("  The confidence interval includes zero, suggesting we cannot rule out\n")
  cat("  the possibility of no relationship in the population.\n")
}
```
