Calculate the difference in correlations for 1) temporality and expectbility and 2) temporality and positive emotion.

    a.	Include the output from the test through Pearson's test.
    b.	Is there a significant difference in their correlations?

```
I compared two dependent correlations sharing the common variable temporality: (1) temporality × expectability and (2) temporality × positive emotion. I calculated all three Pearson correlations needed for the analysis. To test whether the correlations differ significantly, I used Steiger's Z-test for dependent correlations. I calculated the test statistic using the formula that incorporates all three correlations and reported the p-value. I verified results using the cocor package. 

There IS a statistically significant difference between the two correlations (p = 0.0000 < 0.05). Temporality has a STRONGER correlation with expectability (r = 0.2981) than with positive emotion (r = -0.1955).
```

```{r correl2}
temp_data <- noout$temporality
expect_data <- noout$expectability
positive_data <- noout$positive

# Get complete cases for all three variables
complete_cases <- complete.cases(temp_data, expect_data, positive_data)
temp_complete <- temp_data[complete_cases]
expect_complete <- expect_data[complete_cases]
positive_complete <- positive_data[complete_cases]

n <- length(temp_complete)

# a. Include the output from the test through Pearson's test
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# r12: Temporality × Expectability
cor_temp_expect <- cor.test(temp_complete, expect_complete, method = "pearson")
r12 <- cor_temp_expect$estimate

# r13: Temporality × Positive Emotion
cor_temp_positive <- cor.test(temp_complete, positive_complete, method = "pearson")
r13 <- cor_temp_positive$estimate

# r23: Expectability × Positive Emotion (needed for Steiger's test)
cor_expect_positive <- cor.test(expect_complete, positive_complete, method = "pearson")
r23 <- cor_expect_positive$estimate

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", r12), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_temp_expect$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_expect$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_temp_expect$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_temp_expect$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_temp_expect$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_temp_expect$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat("\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_expect$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_expect$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  R² = ", sprintf("%.4f", r12^2), 
    sprintf(" (%.2f%% shared variance)\n\n", 100 * r12^2))

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", r13), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_temp_positive$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_positive$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_temp_positive$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_temp_positive$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_temp_positive$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_temp_positive$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat("\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_positive$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_positive$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  R² = ", sprintf("%.4f", r13^2), 
    sprintf(" (%.2f%% shared variance)\n\n", 100 * r13^2))

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", r23), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_expect_positive$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_expect_positive$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_expect_positive$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_expect_positive$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_expect_positive$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_expect_positive$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat("\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_expect_positive$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_expect_positive$conf.int[2]), "]\n\n", sep = "")

correlation_summary <- data.frame(
  Correlation = c("Temporality × Expectability (r₁₂)",
                  "Temporality × Positive Emotion (r₁₃)",
                  "Expectability × Positive Emotion (r₂₃)"),
  r = c(sprintf("%.4f", r12), sprintf("%.4f", r13), sprintf("%.4f", r23)),
  t = c(sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_expect$statistic),
        sprintf("%.4f", cor_temp_positive$statistic),
        sprintf("%.4f", cor_expect_positive$statistic)),
  p = c(sprintf("%.6f", cor_temp_expect$p.value),
        sprintf("%.6f", cor_temp_positive$p.value),
        sprintf("%.6f", cor_expect_positive$p.value)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(correlation_summary, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\n")

# b. Is there a significant difference in their correlations?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Steiger's Z-test calculation
term1 <- (r12 - r13) * sqrt((n - 3) * (1 + r23))
term2 <- sqrt(2 * (1 - r12^2 - r13^2 - r23^2 + 2*r12*r13*r23))

steiger_t <- term1 / term2

steiger_p <- 2 * (1 - pt(abs(steiger_t), df = n - 3))

cat("Difference in correlations:\n")
diff_r <- r12 - r13
cat("  r₁₂ - r₁₃ =", sprintf("%.4f", diff_r), "\n\n")

cat("Test statistic:\n")
cat("  t(", n - 3, ") = ", sprintf("%.4f", steiger_t), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value (two-tailed) = ", sprintf("%.6f", steiger_p), sep = "")

if(steiger_p < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n\n")
} else if(steiger_p < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n\n")
} else if(steiger_p < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n\n")
} else {
  cat("\n\n")
}

# Install and load cocor package if not available
if(!require(cocor)) {
  install.packages("cocor")
  library(cocor)
}

# Use cocor to compare dependent correlations
cocor_result <- cocor.dep.groups.overlap(
  r.jk = r12,  # Temporality × Expectability
  r.jh = r13,  # Temporality × Positive Emotion
  r.kh = r23,  # Expectability × Positive Emotion
  n = n,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  test = c("steiger1980"),
  return.htest = TRUE
)

cat("cocor package output (Steiger's test):\n")
print(cocor_result)
cat("\n")

alpha <- 0.05
cat("Significance level: α =", alpha, "\n\n")

if(steiger_p < alpha) {
  cat("DECISION: REJECT THE NULL HYPOTHESIS\n\n")
  cat("Conclusion:\n")
  cat("  There IS a statistically significant difference between the two correlations\n")
  cat("  (p = ", sprintf("%.4f", steiger_p), " < ", alpha, ").\n\n", sep = "")
  
  if(abs(r12) > abs(r13)) {
    cat("  Temporality has a STRONGER correlation with expectability (r = ", 
        sprintf("%.4f", r12), ")\n", sep = "")
    cat("  than with positive emotion (r = ", sprintf("%.4f", r13), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  } else {
    cat("  Temporality has a STRONGER correlation with positive emotion (r = ", 
        sprintf("%.4f", r13), ")\n", sep = "")
    cat("  than with expectability (r = ", sprintf("%.4f", r12), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  }
  
} else {
  cat("DECISION: FAIL TO REJECT THE NULL HYPOTHESIS\n\n")
  cat("Conclusion:\n")
  cat("  There is NO statistically significant difference between the two correlations\n")
  cat("  (p = ", sprintf("%.4f", steiger_p), " >= ", alpha, ").\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("  Although r12 = ", sprintf("%.4f", r12), " and r13 = ", sprintf("%.4f", r13), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("  differ numerically by ", sprintf("%.4f", abs(diff_r)), 
      ", this difference could reasonably\n", sep = "")
  cat("  be due to sampling error. We cannot conclude that temporality relates\n")
  cat("  more strongly to one variable than the other.\n\n")
}

# Effect size for the difference
cat("EFFECT SIZE:\n")
cat("------------\n\n")

cat("Absolute difference in correlations:\n")
cat("  |r₁₂ - r₁₃| = ", sprintf("%.4f", abs(diff_r)), "\n\n", sep = "")

if(abs(diff_r) < 0.1) {
  effect_size <- "trivial"
} else if(abs(diff_r) < 0.3) {
  effect_size <- "small"
} else if(abs(diff_r) < 0.5) {
  effect_size <- "medium"
} else {
  effect_size <- "large"
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

barplot(c(r12, r13),
        names.arg = c("Temporality ×\nExpectability", 
                      "Temporality ×\nPositive Emotion"),
        col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
        ylim = c(min(0, min(r12, r13) - 0.1), max(r12, r13) + 0.1),
        main = "Comparison of Correlations",
        ylab = "Pearson's r",
        cex.names = 0.9,
        cex.main = 1.2)

abline(h = 0, lwd = 2)

text(c(0.7, 1.9), c(r12, r13), 
     labels = sprintf("%.4f", c(r12, r13)),
     pos = 3, cex = 1.1, font = 2)

text(1.3, max(r12, r13) * 0.9,
     sprintf("Diff = %.4f\np = %.4f", abs(diff_r), steiger_p),
     cex = 0.9)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

# Plot 2: Confidence intervals
plot(c(1, 2), c(r12, r13),
     xlim = c(0.5, 2.5),
     ylim = c(min(cor_temp_expect$conf.int[1], cor_temp_positive$conf.int[1]) - 0.05,
              max(cor_temp_expect$conf.int[2], cor_temp_positive$conf.int[2]) + 0.05),
     pch = 19,
     cex = 2,
     col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "Correlation Coefficient",
     main = "Correlations with 95% CIs",
     xaxt = "n",
     cex.main = 1.2)

axis(1, at = c(1, 2), 
     labels = c("Temp × Expect", "Temp × Positive"),
     cex.axis = 0.9)

arrows(1, cor_temp_expect$conf.int[1],
       1, cor_temp_expect$conf.int[2],
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")

arrows(2, cor_temp_positive$conf.int[1],
       2, cor_temp_positive$conf.int[2],
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2, col = "coral")

abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

legend("topright",
       legend = "95% CI",
       lwd = 2,
       col = "gray",
       bty = "n",
       cex = 0.9)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

if(steiger_p < alpha) {
  cat("Finding:\n")
  cat("  Temporality shows a significantly stronger relationship with\n")
  if(abs(r12) > abs(r13)) {
    cat("  EXPECTABILITY (satisfaction) than with positive emotion.\n\n")
  } else {
    cat("  POSITIVE EMOTION than with expectability (satisfaction).\n\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("Finding:\n")
  cat("  Temporality relates similarly to both expectability (satisfaction) and\n")
  cat("  positive emotion. The difference between r =", sprintf("%.4f", r12), "\n")
  cat("  and r =", sprintf("%.4f", r13), "is not statistically significant.\n\n")
}
```

Calculate the difference in correlations for gender on temporality and relativity.

    a.	Include the output from the test.
    b.	Is there a significant difference in their correlations?
    
```
I compared the temporality-relativity correlation between women and men, treating them as independent groups. I calculated Pearson correlations separately for each gender. To determine if correlations differ significantly, I used Fisher's Z-test for independent correlations. I verified results using the cocor package. 

There IS a statistically significant difference between the correlations for women and men (p = 0.0003 < .05). MEN show a STRONGER correlation (r =0.2627) between temporality and relativity than WOMEN (r =-0.1817).
```
    
```{r correl3}
women_data <- noout[noout$gender == "women", ]
men_data <- noout[noout$gender == "men", ]

women_complete <- complete.cases(women_data[, c("temporality", "relativity")])
men_complete <- complete.cases(men_data[, c("temporality", "relativity")])

women_temp <- women_data$temporality[women_complete]
women_rel <- women_data$relativity[women_complete]

men_temp <- men_data$temporality[men_complete]
men_rel <- men_data$relativity[men_complete]

n_women <- length(women_temp)
n_men <- length(men_temp)

cat("Sample information:\n")
cat("  Women with complete data:", n_women, "\n")
cat("  Men with complete data:", n_men, "\n")
cat("  Total:", n_women + n_men, "\n\n")

# a. Include the output from the test
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
cor_women <- cor.test(women_temp, women_rel, method = "pearson")
r_women <- cor_women$estimate

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")
cat("  Sample size: n =", n_women, "\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_women$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_women$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_women$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_women$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_women$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_women$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat("\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_women$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_women$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  R² = ", sprintf("%.4f", r_women^2), 
    sprintf(" (%.2f%% shared variance)\n\n", 100 * r_women^2))

# Effect size for women
if(abs(r_women) < 0.1) {
  women_effect <- "negligible"
} else if(abs(r_women) < 0.3) {
  women_effect <- "small"
} else if(abs(r_women) < 0.5) {
  women_effect <- "medium"
} else {
  women_effect <- "large"
}

cat("  Effect size:", women_effect, "\n")
cat("  Direction:", ifelse(r_women > 0, "positive", "negative"), "\n\n")

# Calculate correlation for men
cor_men <- cor.test(men_temp, men_rel, method = "pearson")
r_men <- cor_men$estimate

cat("Pearson's product-moment correlation\n\n")
cat("  Sample size: n =", n_men, "\n")
cat("  r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), "\n")
cat("  t(", cor_men$parameter, ") = ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_men$statistic), "\n", sep = "")
cat("  p-value = ", sprintf("%.6f", cor_men$p.value), sep = "")

if(cor_men$p.value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n")
} else if(cor_men$p.value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n")
} else if(cor_men$p.value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n")
} else {
  cat("\n")
}

cat("  95% CI: [", sprintf("%.4f", cor_men$conf.int[1]), ", ",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_men$conf.int[2]), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("  R² = ", sprintf("%.4f", r_men^2), 
    sprintf(" (%.2f%% shared variance)\n\n", 100 * r_men^2))

# Effect size for men
if(abs(r_men) < 0.1) {
  men_effect <- "negligible"
} else if(abs(r_men) < 0.3) {
  men_effect <- "small"
} else if(abs(r_men) < 0.5) {
  men_effect <- "medium"
} else {
  men_effect <- "large"
}

cat("  Effect size:", men_effect, "\n")
cat("  Direction:", ifelse(r_men > 0, "positive", "negative"), "\n\n")

comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Group = c("Women", "Men"),
  n = c(n_women, n_men),
  r = c(sprintf("%.4f", r_women), sprintf("%.4f", r_men)),
  CI_Lower = c(sprintf("%.4f", cor_women$conf.int[1]), 
               sprintf("%.4f", cor_men$conf.int[1])),
  CI_Upper = c(sprintf("%.4f", cor_women$conf.int[2]), 
               sprintf("%.4f", cor_men$conf.int[2])),
  p_value = c(sprintf("%.6f", cor_women$p.value), 
              sprintf("%.6f", cor_men$p.value)),
  R_squared = c(sprintf("%.4f", r_women^2), sprintf("%.4f", r_men^2)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(comparison_table, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\n")

cat("Difference in correlations:\n")
diff_r <- r_women - r_men
cat("  r_women - r_men =", sprintf("%.4f", diff_r), "\n\n")

# b. Is there a significant difference in their correlations?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fisher's Z transformation
z_women <- 0.5 * log((1 + r_women) / (1 - r_women))
z_men <- 0.5 * log((1 + r_men) / (1 - r_men))

cat("  Women: r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), "→ Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_women), "\n")
cat("  Men:   r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), "→ Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_men), "\n\n")

se_diff <- sqrt(1/(n_women - 3) + 1/(n_men - 3))

cat("  SE =", sprintf("%.4f", se_diff), "\n\n")

z_obs <- (z_women - z_men) / se_diff

cat("  Z_obs =", sprintf("%.4f", z_obs), "\n\n")

p_value <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_obs)))

cat("  p-value =", sprintf("%.6f", p_value))

if(p_value < 0.001) {
  cat(" ***\n\n")
} else if(p_value < 0.01) {
  cat(" **\n\n")
} else if(p_value < 0.05) {
  cat(" *\n\n")
} else {
  cat("\n\n")
}

cat("Fisher's Z-test for independent correlations:\n\n")
cat("  Sample sizes:\n")
cat("    Women: n =", n_women, "\n")
cat("    Men:   n =", n_men, "\n\n")

cat("  Correlations:\n")
cat("    Women: r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), "\n")
cat("    Men:   r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), "\n")
cat("    Difference: Δr =", sprintf("%.4f", diff_r), "\n\n")

cat("  Fisher's Z values:\n")
cat("    Women: Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_women), "\n")
cat("    Men:   Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_men), "\n")
cat("    Difference: ΔZ =", sprintf("%.4f", z_women - z_men), "\n\n")

cat("  Test statistic:\n")
cat("    Z =", sprintf("%.4f", z_obs), "\n\n")

cat("  p-value (two-tailed):\n")
cat("    p =", sprintf("%.6f", p_value), "\n\n")

cat("  95% Confidence interval for the difference:\n")
ci_lower <- (z_women - z_men) - 1.96 * se_diff
ci_upper <- (z_women - z_men) + 1.96 * se_diff

# Transform back to r scale (approximate)
r_diff_lower <- tanh(ci_lower)
r_diff_upper <- tanh(ci_upper)

cat("    In Z scale: [", sprintf("%.4f", ci_lower), ", ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", ci_upper), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("    In r scale (approx): [", sprintf("%.4f", r_diff_lower), ", ", 
    sprintf("%.4f", r_diff_upper), "]\n\n", sep = "")

# Alternative: Using cocor package

# Install and load cocor package if not available
if(!require(cocor)) {
  install.packages("cocor")
  library(cocor)
}

cocor_result <- cocor.indep.groups(
  r1.jk = r_women,
  r2.hm = r_men,
  n1 = n_women,
  n2 = n_men,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  test = c("fisher1925"),
  return.htest = TRUE
)

cat("cocor package output (Fisher's test):\n")
print(cocor_result)
cat("\n")

alpha <- 0.05
cat("Significance level: α =", alpha, "\n\n")

if(p_value < alpha) {
  cat("DECISION: REJECT THE NULL HYPOTHESIS\n\n")
  cat("Conclusion:\n")
  cat("  There IS a statistically significant difference between the correlations\n")
  cat("  for women and men (p =", sprintf("%.4f", p_value), "< .05).\n\n")
  
  if(abs(r_women) > abs(r_men)) {
    cat("  WOMEN show a STRONGER correlation (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), ")\n", sep = "")
    cat("  between temporality and relativity than MEN (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  } else {
    cat("  MEN show a STRONGER correlation (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), ")\n", sep = "")
    cat("  between temporality and relativity than WOMEN (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  }
  
} else {
  cat("DECISION: FAIL TO REJECT THE NULL HYPOTHESIS\n\n")
  cat("Conclusion:\n")
  cat("  There is NO statistically significant difference between the correlations\n")
  cat("  for women and men (p =", sprintf("%.4f", p_value), ">= .05).\n\n")
  cat("  Although women's r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), "and men's r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), "\n")
  cat("  differ numerically by", sprintf("%.4f", abs(diff_r)), ", this difference could\n")
  cat("  reasonably be due to sampling error. Gender does not significantly moderate\n")
  cat("  the relationship between temporality and relativity.\n\n")
}

cat("Absolute difference in correlations:\n")
cat("  |r_women - r_men| =", sprintf("%.4f", abs(diff_r)), "\n\n")

if(abs(diff_r) < 0.1) {
  diff_effect <- "trivial"
} else if(abs(diff_r) < 0.3) {
  diff_effect <- "small"
} else if(abs(diff_r) < 0.5) {
  diff_effect <- "medium"
} else {
  diff_effect <- "large"
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))

barplot(c(r_women, r_men),
        names.arg = c("Women", "Men"),
        col = c("pink", "lightblue"),
        ylim = c(min(0, min(r_women, r_men) - 0.1), max(r_women, r_men) + 0.15),
        main = "Correlation by Gender\nTemporality × Relativity",
        ylab = "Pearson's r",
        cex.names = 1.1,
        cex.main = 1.2)

abline(h = 0, lwd = 2)

text(c(0.7, 1.9), c(r_women, r_men), 
     labels = sprintf("%.4f", c(r_women, r_men)),
     pos = 3, cex = 1.1, font = 2)

text(1.3, max(r_women, r_men) * 0.95,
     sprintf("Diff = %.4f\np = %.4f%s", 
             abs(diff_r), p_value,
             ifelse(p_value < 0.05, " *", "")),
     cex = 0.9)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

plot(c(1, 2), c(r_women, r_men),
     xlim = c(0.5, 2.5),
     ylim = c(min(cor_women$conf.int[1], cor_men$conf.int[1]) - 0.05,
              max(cor_women$conf.int[2], cor_men$conf.int[2]) + 0.05),
     pch = c(19, 17),
     cex = 2,
     col = c("pink", "lightblue"),
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "Correlation Coefficient",
     main = "Correlations with 95% CIs",
     xaxt = "n",
     cex.main = 1.2)

axis(1, at = c(1, 2), 
     labels = c("Women", "Men"),
     cex.axis = 1.1)

arrows(1, cor_women$conf.int[1],
       1, cor_women$conf.int[2],
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 3, col = "red")

arrows(2, cor_men$conf.int[1],
       2, cor_men$conf.int[2],
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 3, col = "blue")

abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray", lwd = 2)

grid(col = "gray", lty = 3)

ci_overlap <- !(cor_women$conf.int[2] < cor_men$conf.int[1] || 
                cor_women$conf.int[1] > cor_men$conf.int[2])

text(1.5, min(cor_women$conf.int[1], cor_men$conf.int[1]) + 0.02,
     ifelse(ci_overlap, "CIs overlap", "CIs do not overlap"),
     cex = 0.9,
     col = ifelse(ci_overlap, "darkgreen", "darkred"))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

if(ci_overlap) {
  cat("Note: The confidence intervals OVERLAP, suggesting the correlations may\n")
  cat("      not be meaningfully different despite any statistical significance.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("Note: The confidence intervals DO NOT OVERLAP, providing additional\n")
  cat("      evidence that the correlations differ between groups.\n\n")
}

if(p_value < alpha) {
  cat("Finding:\n")
  cat("  Gender MODERATES the relationship between temporality and relativity.\n\n")
  
  if(abs(r_women) > abs(r_men)) {
    cat("  For WOMEN, the system's adaptability is more strongly associated with\n")
    cat("  comparative ratings (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), ") than for MEN (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  } else {
    cat("  For MEN, the system's adaptability is more strongly associated with\n")
    cat("  comparative ratings (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), ") than for WOMEN (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), ").\n\n", sep = "")
  }
} else {
  cat("Finding:\n")
  cat("  Gender DOES NOT moderate the relationship between temporality and relativity.\n\n")
  cat("  Both women (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_women), ") and men (r =", sprintf("%.4f", r_men), ")\n", sep = "")
  cat("  show similar correlations between system adaptability and comparative ratings.\n\n")
}
```

Calculate the partial and semipartial correlations for all variables, and include the output. 
    a.	Are any of the correlations significant after controlling for all other relationships?
    
```
I calculated partial and semipartial correlations for all four continuous variables (temporality, expectability, relativity, positive). I displayed complete correlation matrices with significance tests and compared zero-order (no controls), partial, and semipartial correlations side-by-side. For each variable pair, I identified which control variables were partialed out, calculated how much correlations were reduced when controls were applied, and determined significance. I identified which partial correlations have p < .05, reported them in a table, and concluded YES with specific pairs if any remain significant, or NO if none survive controlling for other variables. 

YES - The following correlations are significant after controlling for all other relationships:

  1. temporality × expectability (r = 0.2573, p = 0.000025)
  2. temporality × relativity (r = 0.1698, p = 0.005861)
  3. temporality × positive (r = -0.1821, p = 0.003097)
  4. expectability × relativity (r = 0.1704, p = 0.005690)
```
    
```{r partials}
if(!require(ppcor)) {
  install.packages("ppcor")
  library(ppcor)
}

continuous_vars <- c("temporality", "expectability", "relativity", "positive")
cor_data <- noout[, continuous_vars]

cor_data_complete <- na.omit(cor_data)
n_complete <- nrow(cor_data_complete)

# Zero-order correlations (for reference)
zero_order <- cor(cor_data_complete, method = "pearson")

cat("Correlation Matrix:\n")
cat("-------------------\n")
print(round(zero_order, 4))
cat("\n")

n_vars <- ncol(cor_data_complete)
for(i in 1:(n_vars-1)) {
  for(j in (i+1):n_vars) {
    test_result <- cor.test(cor_data_complete[, i], cor_data_complete[, j])
    
    cat(sprintf("%s × %s:\n", continuous_vars[i], continuous_vars[j]))
    cat(sprintf("  r = %.4f, t(%d) = %.4f, p = %.6f", 
                test_result$estimate, 
                test_result$parameter,
                test_result$statistic,
                test_result$p.value))
    
    if(test_result$p.value < 0.001) cat(" ***\n")
    else if(test_result$p.value < 0.01) cat(" **\n")
    else if(test_result$p.value < 0.05) cat(" *\n")
    else cat("\n")
  }
}
cat("\n")

# PARTIAL CORRELATIONS
partial_results <- pcor(cor_data_complete, method = "pearson")

partial_cor <- partial_results$estimate
rownames(partial_cor) <- continuous_vars
colnames(partial_cor) <- continuous_vars

print(round(partial_cor, 4))
cat("\n")

partial_pval <- partial_results$p.value
rownames(partial_pval) <- continuous_vars
colnames(partial_pval) <- continuous_vars

print(round(partial_pval, 6))
cat("\n")

partial_formatted <- matrix("", nrow = n_vars, ncol = n_vars)
rownames(partial_formatted) <- continuous_vars
colnames(partial_formatted) <- continuous_vars

for(i in 1:n_vars) {
  for(j in 1:n_vars) {
    if(i == j) {
      partial_formatted[i, j] <- "1.0000"
    } else {
      r_val <- partial_cor[i, j]
      p_val <- partial_pval[i, j]
      
      if(p_val < 0.001) {
        partial_formatted[i, j] <- sprintf("%.4f***", r_val)
      } else if(p_val < 0.01) {
        partial_formatted[i, j] <- sprintf("%.4f** ", r_val)
      } else if(p_val < 0.05) {
        partial_formatted[i, j] <- sprintf("%.4f*  ", r_val)
      } else {
        partial_formatted[i, j] <- sprintf("%.4f   ", r_val)
      }
    }
  }
}

print(partial_formatted, quote = FALSE)
cat("\nSignificance: *** p < .001, ** p < .01, * p < .05\n\n")

pair_count <- 1
for(i in 1:(n_vars-1)) {
  for(j in (i+1):n_vars) {
    var1 <- continuous_vars[i]
    var2 <- continuous_vars[j]
    
    control_vars <- continuous_vars[-c(i, j)]
    
    r_partial <- partial_cor[i, j]
    p_partial <- partial_pval[i, j]
    
    r_zero <- zero_order[i, j]
    
    cat(sprintf("Pair %d: %s × %s\n", pair_count, var1, var2))
    cat(sprintf("  Controlling for: %s\n", paste(control_vars, collapse = ", ")))
    cat(sprintf("  Zero-order r:  %.4f\n", r_zero))
    cat(sprintf("  Partial r:     %.4f\n", r_partial))
    cat(sprintf("  Difference:    %.4f\n", r_zero - r_partial))
    cat(sprintf("  p-value:       %.6f", p_partial))
    
    if(p_partial < 0.001) cat(" ***\n")
    else if(p_partial < 0.01) cat(" **\n")
    else if(p_partial < 0.05) cat(" *\n")
    else cat(" (not significant)\n")
    
    if(p_partial < 0.05) {
      cat("  Significant: YES - The relationship remains after controlling for other variables.\n")
    } else {
      cat("  Significant: NO - The relationship disappears after controlling for other variables.\n")
    }
    
    cat("\n")
    pair_count <- pair_count + 1
  }
}

# a. Are any of the correlations significant after controlling for all other relationships?

)

      ))

}

                significant_partials$Partial_r[k],

}

reduction_results <- data.frame(
  Pair = character(),
  Zero_Order = numeric(),
  Partial = numeric(),
  Reduction = numeric(),
  Percent_Reduction = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for(i in 1:(n_vars-1)) {

    pair_name <- paste(continuous_vars[i], "×", continuous_vars[j])
    
    r_zero <- zero_order[i, j]
    r_partial <- partial_cor[i, j]
    reduction <- abs(r_zero) - abs(r_partial)
    pct_reduction <- (reduction / abs(r_zero)) * 100
    
    reduction_results <- rbind(reduction_results, data.frame(
      Pair = pair_name,
      Zero_Order = round(r_zero, 4),
      Partial = round(r_partial, 4),
      Reduction = round(reduction, 4),
      Percent_Reduction = round(pct_reduction, 2),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

print(reduction_results, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Theory:

    - What are we using as our model for understanding the data in a correlational analysis?
    
```
In correlational analysis, we use a linear model assuming variables relate through straight-line relationships (Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε). The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) represents the standardized strength and direction of this linear association. For multiple variables, the correlation matrix serves as our model, capturing all pairwise relationships and assuming multivariate normality.
```
    
    - How might we determine model fit?
    
```
Model fit is assessed through scatterplots (points should cluster around a line), residual plots (random scatter), comparing linear vs. LOESS curves, and r² (variance explained). For multiple correlations, use Bartlett's test (variables are correlated), KMO measure (sampling adequacy > 0.6), and the correlation matrix determinant (checks multicollinearity). Also examine confidence intervals, significance tests, and effect sizes (Cohen's: small = .10-.29, medium = .30-.49, large ≥ .50).
```
    
    - What is the difference between correlation and covariance?
    
```
Covariance measures the direction and magnitude of linear relationships but is unstandardized (depends on variable scales), ranges from -∞ to +∞, and is difficult to interpret. Correlation is standardized covariance: r = Cov(X,Y)/(SD_X × SD_Y). It's unit-free, ranges from -1 to +1, and allows meaningful comparisons across different variable pairs. We use correlation because it's interpretable regardless of measurement scales.
```
    
    - What is the difference between R and r?
    
```
r is the bivariate correlation between two variables, ranging from -1 to +1. R is the multiple correlation i.e. the correlation between observed outcomes and predictions from multiple regression with several predictors, ranging from 0 to +1 (always positive). R² represents the proportion of variance explained by all predictors combined.
```
    
    - When would I want to use a nonparametric correlation over Pearson's correlation?
    
```
We want to use nonparametric correlations (Spearman's ρ or Kendall's τ) when: (1) we have ordinal data or ranks, (2) distributions are non-normal with skewness or outliers, (3) relationships are monotonic but not linear, or (4) sample sizes are small with questionable normality. Nonparametric methods work with ranks rather than raw values, making them robust to outliers and assumption violations. Pearson's r is more powerful when assumptions are met, so it is prefered for continuous, normally distributed data with linear relationships.


```
    
    - What is the distinction between semi-partial and partial correlations? 
    
```
Partial correlation removes control variables' effects from both variables in the pair. Semipartial correlation removes controls from only one variable. Partial correlations are larger in absolute value because removing variance from both variables strengthens their purified relationship. Wew want to use partial when examining direct relationships independent of confounds and semipartial when determining unique variance contribution.
```
